This map does not show whether a test has been ordered, booked or completed. Do not wait for a scheduled test if you develop new symptoms.
This is a visual orientation, not a prediction of your personal cycle. It shows when some effects often emerge and which effects are not tied to a particular day.

Cisplatin precedes the same-day radiation session.

Days 1–21Symptoms can build during treatment and continue afterwards.
Symptoms can build during treatment and continue afterwards.
There are no guaranteed “safe days”. Your prescription and team’s instructions take priority. Contact the team about new symptoms rather than waiting for a scheduled visit.
Safety review, anti-sickness medicines, fluids and cisplatin; radiation follows as arranged. Confirm both appointments; tell staff if radiation has been cancelled.
Follow the separate radiation calendar, oral care, drinking and nutrition plan. Call for symptoms early and arrange blood tests before the next cisplatin.
Agree the arrangements with your oncology team.
Confirm the exact regimen, treatment aim, baseline tests, transport, support medicines and actual urgent contact numbers. Bring any hearing concerns, swallowing problems and medicine list.
Radiation appointments are separate from medicine visits. Keep one calendar showing both departments and tests; tell the team promptly about a cancelled session.
Tell the team about travel, cost, work, caring responsibilities, communication or reading needs. Ask whether a support person or interpreter can attend and how treatment changes will be explained.
Check the next visit and blood-test dates, support medicines and who to call if unwell. Have the team replace example phone numbers before using the wallet card.
Ask for one schedule showing prevention medicines, rescue treatment and what to do if symptoms persist. Do not add, double or restart medicines from an old prescription.
NCCP 00387 specifically recommends dentistry and nutrition consultation before treatment. It also encourages oral hydration for 24 hours after cisplatin, adapted to your individual fluid plan.

Cisplatin needs prescribed fluids before and after infusion. Follow the team’s drinking advice and report much less urine, vomiting or inability to drink. Do not change fluid intake or diuretics without advice.

A dietitian can tailor food texture, supplements and calorie or protein needs. Tell the team early if eating or drinking becomes difficult; do not wait for substantial weight loss. Fluid targets depend on kidney and heart health.

Use the mouth-care plan provided by the team and tell them about ulcers, thrush, bleeding or pain. Inform your dentist about cancer treatment. Before any dental procedure, confirm timing with the oncology team.

A speech and language therapist can assess swallowing and advise exercises or safer food and drink textures. Follow the individual assessment; a general guide cannot decide which textures are safe for you.

Discuss fertility and pregnancy precautions before treatment and the medicine-specific duration of contraception afterwards. Ask about breastfeeding. Bring a full medicine, supplement and allergy list; check before adding over-the-counter or herbal products.
Keep your pathology and agreed treatment goal with your records.

Ask which part of the head or neck the cancer started in, what the biopsy shows and how far it has spread. Site, stage, previous treatment and your health affect the options. HPV/p16 testing is relevant to some sites; it is not the same test as PD-L1.
Locally advanced stage III–IV squamous head and neck cancer. This guide should match the named treatment on your prescription.

Your team explains any HPV/p16, Epstein–Barr virus or other tumour tests relevant to your cancer site. Not every head and neck cancer needs the same tests; the medicine safety checks are a separate matter.
The consent conversation explains the boundaries of the plan.

Cisplatin and radiotherapy work together to treat locally advanced head and neck cancer. Your team explains the treatment aim, likely benefit and alternatives for your diagnosis. Ask how alternatives compare for your health, goals and previous treatment. A study result cannot predict an individual outcome.

The clinician may delay, change or stop treatment because of symptoms, test results or your priorities. Record which component is affected and what is needed before restarting. Do not restart from an old prescription.
Radiotherapy treats a planned local area while medicine supports the cancer treatment. The radiation prescription, number of sessions and late-effect plan are agreed separately.
Plan the appointments and support around the prescribed schedule.
If radiation is cancelled, cisplatin is withheld until radiation resumes. Ask both departments to confirm revised dates; do not assume the chemotherapy visit proceeds unchanged.
Write the actual treatment date, phase and any change. The wallet card is a brief record; the passport holds the fuller history. It does not replace the hospital treatment record.
Use the agreed home plan and contact pathway.
Some effects appear soon after treatment and others build over weeks. Do not wait for the next appointment if a symptom is new, severe or worsening.

Keep prevention, rescue and regular medicines clearly separated on one written list. Record what you have taken and the response, so the team can adjust it. Do not double a missed dose unless your prescriber tells you to.

Contact oncology promptly for fever, sudden illness, persistent vomiting, much less urine, severe mouth pain or inability to drink. Report hearing change, ringing in the ears or new numbness before the next dose. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain or collapse is an emergency.
Dental preparation and gentle daily care reduce avoidable problems.

Arrange dental assessment before head and neck radiation. The dental and oncology teams decide what treatment is needed and how much healing time is required; do not schedule extractions independently.

Follow the prescribed brushing, fluoride, rinse and pain-relief advice. Report ulcers, infection, new bleeding, difficulty wearing dentures or worsening jaw opening. Avoid starting a new mouthwash without checking if the mouth is sore.

Dry mouth can increase dental problems and some radiation effects last. Keep regular dental care and tell any future dentist that you have had head and neck radiation before invasive treatment. Your radiation/dental team plans any procedure.
The aim is adequate intake and comfort during treatment.
Record weight and report food or drink becoming harder to manage. Pain, taste change, dry mouth or nausea can each need a different response; a dietitian can adapt the plan to you.

The team may suggest food fortification, supplements or tube feeding when intake or swallowing safety requires it. A tube is a support option, not a judgement about how well you have tried to eat. Training and follow-up are needed.
Ask for a realistic drinking plan that accounts for kidney/heart problems and any feeding tube. Persistent vomiting, dizziness, markedly reduced urine or inability to drink needs urgent contact.
A speech and language therapist can help protect function.
Report coughing or choking with food or drink, a wet-sounding voice after swallowing, food sticking or repeated chest infections. The team may need to assess aspiration risk and safe textures.
Do swallowing or jaw exercises only as taught for your situation. Treatment and recovery can change what is comfortable and safe. Ask for reassessment when symptoms change.
Tell the team about changes in speech, voice or hearing. Ask for written instructions, communication aids, an interpreter or help involving a support person.
Practical adjustments can make the plan easier to follow.
Balance rest with manageable activity according to your ability and team advice. Ask for help if weakness, falls, sleep difficulty or pain interferes with daily life.
Ask for support to stop smoking and discuss alcohol with the team. Mouth irritation, medicine interactions and head and neck recovery can change what is safe for you.

Tell the team about anxiety, appearance or intimacy concerns, finances, travel and caring responsibilities. Ask which local supports are available; resources can be added to your record when confirmed.
Treatment completion and recovery are different milestones.

Your team sets examinations and imaging around the disease, treatment and symptoms. Record who arranges each test and who explains the result. An unbooked scan is not automatically due at a fixed week because a general guide says so.
Keep the regimen name, last treatment date, ongoing medicines and relevant alert card. Tell clinicians about earlier immune treatment or head and neck radiation even after the course has ended.
Keep essential instructions available on paper.

The three-page companion gives the essentials. Use the passport for the agreed plan, visits, test results, symptoms and questions. The wallet QR opens this exact treatment’s further information; it contains no personal clinical record.

The phone numbers printed as examples must be replaced and checked by the treating service. Add the unit’s daytime, out-of-hours and backup route; keep this information where you and a support person can find it.

Use the full printable handbook in its chapter order and write questions in the passport. You do not need to scan the QR or follow an internet link to use the essential treatment and safety information.
Cisplatin is used with radiotherapy under the exact NCCP indication and schedule.

RTOG 91-11 supports concurrent cisplatin-radiotherapy for preservation and local control of the larynx in its selected laryngeal-cancer population. It did not show an overall-survival advantage across its three groups. The long-term report also raised concerns about deaths unrelated to larynx cancer. These findings cannot be presented as a survival benefit across every head and neck site.

Blood count, kidney and liver function; audiology and measured creatinine clearance when indicated. Review hearing, tinnitus, nerve symptoms and medicines. Dental and nutrition preparation and a swallowing plan are important before head and neck radiotherapy. Blood count, kidney and liver function before every cisplatin cycle. Report hearing or tinnitus and nerve changes before each dose; audiology is repeated when indicated. Review weight, drinking, swallowing, mouth and skin symptoms during the radiation course.
The team records the reason and recovery or tests needed before restarting. Do not count an omitted dose as completed or restart from an old plan.

Record each cycle separately. Each medicine has its own symptom table. Mark the worst symptoms since your last review, when they occurred and what they stopped you doing. Overlapping symptoms can be recorded under more than one medicine; you do not have to identify the cause.

Use a new record sheet for each cycle or review. Copy or print another sheet when needed; the number of sheets does not prescribe the length of treatment.

Cetuximab + cisplatin + fluorouracilNational Cancer Control Programme (NCCP) 00417

Record each cycle separately. Each medicine has its own symptom table. Mark the worst symptoms since your last review, when they occurred and what they stopped you doing. Overlapping symptoms can be recorded under more than one medicine; you do not have to identify the cause.

These are patient-language severity prompts, not a validated questionnaire or a formal Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grading tool. Your team assigns the clinical grade. Serious symptoms override the columns: call without waiting to decide a severity level.
Use a new record sheet for each cycle or review. Copy or print another sheet when needed; the number of sheets does not prescribe the length of treatment.
Record the date, medicines actually received, delays or omissions, test results and concerns with your team. Use a separate record for any changed treatment phase.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, persistent vomiting, diarrhoea, severe mouth pain or inability to drink. Chest pain during or after fluorouracil, or unusually early severe symptoms, needs urgent assessment even if dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (a medicine-processing enzyme) (DPD) testing was normal. Report breathing difficulty, swelling, faintness, spreading skin infection or painful eyes promptly. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Cetuximab with cisplatin and fluorouracil is used to treat squamous head and neck cancer. Discuss the individual aim, likely benefit, symptom control and alternatives with your oncology team.

Cetuximab attaches to the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) on cells and blocks growth signals. It is combined with chemotherapy in this plan. Healthy skin and nails also depend on this pathway, explaining some of the characteristic rash, dryness and nail problems. This is a different treatment from checkpoint immunotherapy.
What to watch forTell staff immediately about itching, flushing, swelling, wheeze or faintness. Report skin infection, eye pain, new breathlessness or marked cramps.

Cisplatin links strands of DNA, the instructions inside cells, making it harder for cancer cells to repair damage and divide. Healthy cells may also be affected. Kidney function, hearing, blood counts and nerve symptoms help the team decide whether the next dose is safe.
What to watch forReport reduced urine, persistent vomiting, tinnitus, hearing change or new tingling.

Fluorouracil, often shortened to 5-FU, interferes with the building blocks used to make DNA and RNA, which cells need to grow. It runs through a vein over the prescribed hours. Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) is an enzyme that breaks it down. Testing for DPD deficiency before treatment reduces risk but cannot rule out every severe reaction.
What to watch forReport severe diarrhoea, mouth sores, chest pain, sudden confusion, sore palms or soles, or unexpectedly early severe symptoms.

Your team confirms the active stage and dates. The full treatment guide explains each step.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.

Cisplatin is given on Day 1, fluorouracil on Days 1–4, and cetuximab on Days 1, 8 and 15 of each 21-day cycle, for up to 6 combination cycles. The team may then consider weekly cetuximab alone under a separate maintenance plan (NCCP 00207). This is not an automatic continuation.
These cetuximab-only visits remain part of the same combination cycle. Continue the skin, allergy and symptom checks; use the prescribed visit-specific support plan.

The source allows consideration of cetuximab alone after the combination course, under NCCP 00207. Ask for a separate calendar and support/monitoring plan. The six combination stamps do not record maintenance.
Visits within a cycle are not separate courses. The team records delays, omitted doses and any change of plan. A stamp records completed treatment; it does not authorise the next dose.
Required regimen tests, symptom-triggered investigations and cancer-response tests serve different purposes. Ask who books each test and who explains the result.
Checks infection-fighting cells, oxygen-carrying cells and platelets.
Guide safe treatment and identify organ problems.

Checks for reduced ability to break down fluorouracil; results affect treatment choice or dose. Testing cannot exclude every severe reaction. Kidney impairment can affect one blood-based test, so the team chooses the appropriate method.
Investigates hearing loss or tinnitus and helps judge platinum-related risk.
Records the heart’s electrical activity. New chest symptoms require assessment even after a reassuring earlier test.
Detects mineral changes caused by cetuximab; low levels may cause cramps, weakness or heart-rhythm problems.
Assesses the cancer rather than whether a treatment-day blood count is safe.
Locally advanced or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.
Blood and organ checksNCCP

Full blood count, kidney and liver tests and magnesium; DPD testing before fluorouracil unless already tested. Review previous antibody reactions, red-meat allergy, tick bites and any cetuximab allergy-test results. An ECG is indicated with compromised heart function; hearing tests and creatinine clearance are arranged when indicated.

Full blood count, kidney and liver tests and magnesium before each cycle. Check skin, eyes, bowel symptoms and infusion reactions. Ask about hearing, tinnitus, tingling and hydration at each cycle. Report symptoms before every weekly cetuximab visit, even when chemotherapy is not scheduled.
Report new symptoms promptly; extra tests may be needed.
A held or changed dose needs a new clinical review and relevant repeat results.

After the final cetuximab dose, electrolytes including magnesium and calcium are checked monthly for 2 months. Continue review of persistent skin, kidney, hearing, nerve and nutritional problems. Disease examinations and scans are individually planned.
Treatment and appointmentsNCCP
Confirm the diagnosis, aim, prescription and actual calendar.

Cetuximab starts with a 400 mg/m² loading dose over 120 minutes, then 250 mg/m² over 60 minutes weekly. Chemotherapy starts at least 1 hour after cetuximab finishes. Cisplatin 100 mg/m² is given over 2 hours on Day 1 with prescribed fluids before and after. Fluorouracil is 1,000 mg/m² over 22 hours daily on Days 1–4, or the alternative 2,000 mg/m² over 46–48 hours repeated on Days 3–4. Staff confirm the chosen pump schedule. Plan for monitoring during and for at least 1 hour after each cetuximab infusion under the current medicine information; confirm the observation plan with your unit.
Follow the written home plan and keep pump or line appointments where applicable.
Record the last dose and follow-up appointments.
Mouth, weight and swallowingNCCP
Review oral health, weight, nutrition and safe swallowing.
Discuss mouth pain, intake, weight and hydration.
Report poor drinking, choking or weight loss promptly.
Dietitian and swallowing plans change with symptoms and recovery.
Continue dental, nutritional and swallowing support when needed.

Agree staging, pathology and any relevant disease tests.
Discuss symptoms and the planned response review.
Scans or examinations may be added if symptoms require them.
The team sets imaging and cancer-assessment timing.
No universal imaging interval or routine tumour-marker panel is imposed by this regimen.

There are no guaranteed “safe days”. Your prescription and team’s instructions take priority. Contact the team about new symptoms rather than waiting for a scheduled visit.
Daily 22-hour fluorouracil on Days 1–4, or 2,000 mg/m² over 46–48 hours twice as prescribed; confirm changes and completion. Check the pump appointments and contact the unit for problems.
Cetuximab is due on Days 8 and 15 after review. Other days are not automatically free of side effects. Report diarrhoea, mouth pain, rash, allergy symptoms or poor drinking before each visit.
Continue symptom monitoring and arrange the blood tests required for the next cycle. Ask for revised dates after any hold or delay.
From preparing the line to coming home after disconnection. Your team arranges the appointments and shows you what to do.
Your team selects the access device and teaches its care, including a port or peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) if used.
Daily 22-hour fluorouracil on Days 1–4, or 2,000 mg/m² over 46–48 hours twice as prescribed; confirm changes and completion.
Only trained staff connect, program or change the infusion. Do not calculate or alter the rate yourself.
Call for leakage, pain, swelling, damage, disconnection, unexpected completion or a pump that appears not to run. Follow the unit’s device-specific emergency instructions.
Completion depends on the actual start time and chosen infusion duration. Do not disconnect or reconnect the line yourself.
A line may remain between treatments. Keep dressing, flushing and review appointments and report redness, pain, fever or swelling.

A port is a small chamber beneath the skin, usually on the chest, attached to a tube ending in a large vein. A special needle goes through the skin into the port when it is used. A PICC enters a vein in the upper arm; a short section remains outside under a dressing. Both can deliver a home infusion. Your team helps choose the device and teaches its care.

Tell the team about allergies, blood thinners, infections and any other cancer medicines. Follow the instructions about eating, drinking and transport; do not stop medicines yourself. Port placement uses local anaesthetic, sometimes with sedation or general anaesthetic. The team explains the procedure and risks, including infection, bleeding, clots and insertion complications. Ask how to manage discomfort, protect the wound and resume activity. Report increasing pain, redness, swelling, discharge or fever.

The nurse checks the line and treatment, secures the connection and dressing, and starts the pump. Before leaving, you should have the disconnection location and time, contact numbers including out of hours, and the written spill instructions. Ask to be shown what normal pump progress looks like. You do not need to calculate a rate.

Use the supplied carrier and the position recommended for your pump. Keep tubing free from pulling and kinks. Ask how to place the pump safely for sleep and how to protect the line and dressing when washing. Do not immerse it or swim. Avoid direct heat and cold. An elastomeric pump has a balloon that shrinks slowly and may have no alarm; an electronic pump has different instructions. Follow the instructions for the device you actually receive.

Keep the appointment even if the pump looks empty, unless the team changes the plan. Staff check the pump and line and arrange safe disposal. After flushing and other line care as required, the port needle may be removed and a small dressing applied. The implanted port stays in place until a separate removal procedure is arranged. A PICC remains in place and needs scheduled dressing and flushing care.

Call the team immediately if the pump leaks, is damaged, finishes unexpectedly early, appears not to run, or the line disconnects. Follow the emergency or spill steps you have been specifically taught, including use of a clamp if instructed. Do not reconnect, change settings or disconnect the pump yourself. Keep other people away from leaked medicine. If medicine touches skin, rinse it off and wash with soap and water, then seek advice.

Contact oncology immediately for pain or swelling around the line, a wet/loose dressing, redness, fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell. A painful swollen arm or neck needs urgent advice. Severe chest pain, major breathing difficulty or collapse: call 112 / 999. Do not wait for pump disconnection or the next clinic visit.
Agree the arrangements with your oncology team.
Bring your medicines and allergy list, test dates, treatment calendar and actual emergency contacts. Tell the unit about swallowing, hearing, mobility, transport or communication needs.
Check the next treatment and test dates, medicines, pump or line appointments, and who to contact if unwell. Have the team replace and verify every example phone number on the wallet card.
Ask about transport, work, costs, caring responsibilities, an interpreter or a support person. Keep changes to the plan in one record.

Ask for one list separating prevention medicines, rescue treatment and regular medicines. The schedule must match this treatment and visit. Record what you take and whether it helps; do not double a dose, restart an old prescription or add medicines without checking.

This platinum-containing combination needs an agreed anti-sickness plan. Take prevention medicines at the stated times and keep rescue instructions available. Contact the team for persistent vomiting or inability to drink.

An antihistamine and corticosteroid are given before cetuximab to reduce reaction risk. They do not prevent every reaction. Report itching, flushing, swelling, wheeze, dizziness or faintness immediately, including symptoms that start after leaving the unit.

Use the skin-care plan from the team, including moisturising and sun protection. Report painful cracks, inflamed nails, pus or spreading redness. Eye pain or visual change needs prompt review. Keep prescribed blood tests for magnesium and other minerals; supplements must follow clinical advice.

Cisplatin requires prescribed intravenous fluids and mineral replacement when indicated. Follow the team’s drinking advice and report much less urine, persistent vomiting or difficulty drinking. Do not alter fluids or water tablets yourself.
Tell the team early about reduced intake or weight loss. A dietitian can adapt food texture, supplements and intake goals. Follow an individual fluid plan, especially with kidney or heart problems.

Follow the mouth-care and pain-relief plan. Report ulcers, thrush or swallowing difficulty early. Ask for a swallowing assessment if food or drinks make you cough or choke; do not assume a general food texture is safe for you.

Before treatment, discuss fertility, contraception, pregnancy and breastfeeding, including medicine-specific precautions after treatment. Bring all prescription, over-the-counter and herbal medicines to review. The team must check interactions and allergies.
Keep the pathology, stage and agreed treatment aim with your records.

Ask which head or neck site the cancer started in, what the biopsy shows, how far it has spread and how previous treatment affects the options. HPV/p16 tests apply to some tumour sites; they are different from tests of chemotherapy safety.
Treatment of locally advanced or metastatic squamous cell cancer of the head and neck.

A scan or a tumour-specific test assesses the cancer. Blood counts and kidney or liver tests assess treatment safety. DPD testing concerns fluorouracil metabolism and is not a measure of cancer response.
The consent discussion sets out the personal aim and boundaries.

Cetuximab with cisplatin and fluorouracil is used to treat squamous head and neck cancer. Discuss the individual aim, likely benefit, symptom control and alternatives with your oncology team. Ask about reasonable alternatives, including supportive care, and which outcomes matter most to you. A research result cannot predict an individual outcome.

The team may delay, reduce, omit or stop a medicine after symptoms or test results, a change in benefit or your preference. Record which medicine is affected and what is required before restarting. Do not use an old prescription to restart treatment.

Surgery or radiotherapy may have a separate role, but they are not automatically added to this infusion calendar. For a locally advanced plan, ask whether any part of treatment is outside its current licensed indication and why it is recommended.
Use the medicine schedule and logistics pages for the exact visit pattern.

Check that the treatment name, planned tests, support medicines, transport and urgent contacts are correct. Explain any previous infusion reaction or change in your health before the medicine is prepared.
A missed or held dose is not a completed dose. Ask for revised blood-test, treatment and pump dates where relevant. The team must clarify whether an omitted weekly dose changes later dates.
Record the actual date and medicines received, dose changes, test results and symptoms. The wallet is a brief portable record; the passport holds more detail and does not replace hospital records.
Symptoms do not follow a guaranteed calendar.

Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, persistent vomiting, diarrhoea, severe mouth pain or inability to drink. Chest pain during or after fluorouracil, or unusually early severe symptoms, needs urgent assessment even if DPD testing was normal. Report breathing difficulty, swelling, faintness, spreading skin infection or painful eyes promptly. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency.

Keep prevention, rescue and regular medicines separately labelled. Note doses actually taken and whether symptoms improve. Check new prescription, over-the-counter and herbal medicines with the team; do not add or repeat old courses without advice.

Report numbness, tingling, weakness, falls, difficulty doing buttons or changes in walking. Describe what you can no longer do, not just a symptom score. The team may need to change treatment before symptoms worsen.
This is the home for detailed mouth and dental advice.
Use the prescribed gentle oral-care and pain-relief plan. Report ulcers, infection, bleeding or pain that affects eating or drinking. Check with oncology before dental procedures.

If you have had head and neck radiation, tell your dentist before invasive treatment. Continue the advised preventive care because effects on saliva, teeth and healing can persist. If you have not had radiation, follow the plan for your current treatment.
Adapt the plan to what you can manage safely.

Record changes in weight and what limits eating: soreness, taste change, dry mouth, nausea or fatigue may need different help. A dietitian can adapt meals, supplements or feeding support. Do not wait for substantial weight loss to ask for review.

Contact the team for persistent vomiting, dizziness, much less urine, inability to drink or severe diarrhoea. Fluid goals depend on kidney and heart health. If a feeding tube is needed, ask for training, supplies and a clear problem-contact route.
Protect safe swallowing and make communication easier.

Report coughing or choking with food or drinks, a wet voice after swallowing, food sticking or repeated chest infections. Ask for speech and language assessment; use only the textures and exercises recommended for you.
Tell the team about hearing, speech or voice changes. Request written instructions, an interpreter, communication aids or help involving a support person when useful.
Use the support available around you.

Discuss the level of activity you can manage, work, travel and help at home. Ask for assessment if fatigue, pain, weakness or falls disrupt ordinary activities. Bring practical barriers to appointments into the discussion.

Ask about fertility preservation before treatment and specific pregnancy, contraception and breastfeeding precautions. Tell the team about anxiety, body-image, sexual or relationship concerns; support can be tailored to your priorities.
Ask for help with smoking cessation and discuss alcohol with the team. Mouth symptoms, medicines and recovery may affect what is appropriate for you.
Finishing scheduled doses and recovering are different milestones.
Record who arranges examinations, scans and any tumour-specific tests, and who explains the results. A general reference calendar does not set an appointment or mean a scan is overdue.

Keep the regimen name, last treatment date, current medicines and unresolved side effects available. Tell future clinicians about any earlier head and neck radiotherapy, platinum-related hearing or kidney problems, and significant infusion reactions.
Essential information should remain usable on paper.

Use the passport for the fuller record and the wallet card for the treatment name, contacts and actual completed cycles. Its QR opens this treatment’s information; it does not contain a personal medical record or update paper stamps.
Every example telephone number must be replaced and checked by the treating service before patient use. Add daytime, out-of-hours and backup contacts and keep them accessible to a support person.

Read the full handbook in its chapter sequence. The treatment, symptom, contact and practical information does not require scanning a QR or following a hyperlink. Add questions to the passport and bring it to review.
The EXTREME study tested adding cetuximab to platinum and fluorouracil for recurrent or metastatic squamous head and neck cancer.

The study supports this approach in an appropriate setting. The reported results pooled the platinum options; they are not a separate randomised survival estimate for this particular platinum or for a curative treatment plan. Population: Recurrent or metastatic disease; the study used either cisplatin or carboplatin. Comparison: Platinum and fluorouracil with or without cetuximab. Study populations and individual circumstances differ. The study does not establish that cisplatin and carboplatin give identical outcomes. The current regimen and an individually agreed plan govern treatment duration.

Cetuximab with cisplatin and fluorouracil is used to treat squamous head and neck cancer. Discuss the individual aim, likely benefit, symptom control and alternatives with your oncology team. Ask your team to write down the individual aim and explain reasonable alternatives, their burdens and the uncertainties before you decide.

Cisplatin is given on Day 1, fluorouracil on Days 1–4, and cetuximab on Days 1, 8 and 15 of each 21-day cycle, for up to 6 combination cycles. The team may then consider weekly cetuximab alone under a separate maintenance plan (NCCP 00207). This is not an automatic continuation. Full blood count, kidney and liver tests and magnesium before each cycle. Check skin, eyes, bowel symptoms and infusion reactions. Ask about hearing, tinnitus, tingling and hydration at each cycle. Report symptoms before every weekly cetuximab visit, even when chemotherapy is not scheduled. Confirm the actual dates with your unit.

Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, persistent vomiting, diarrhoea, severe mouth pain or inability to drink. Chest pain during or after fluorouracil, or unusually early severe symptoms, needs urgent assessment even if DPD testing was normal. Report breathing difficulty, swelling, faintness, spreading skin infection or painful eyes promptly. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency. Have the team replace the example numbers with verified daytime, out-of-hours and backup contacts before using the card.

Your team reviews symptoms, test results, treatment benefit and your priorities. Ask when cancer-response assessment is planned and what would lead to a change. A delay or omitted dose must be recorded and does not count as treatment received.

Ask for a written support-medicine plan and early help with mouth pain, eating, drinking, swallowing, skin or nerve symptoms. Tell the team about travel, work, caring and communication needs. Dietitian, speech and language, nursing and other support can be arranged according to your needs.

Give an antihistamine and a corticosteroid at least one hour before cetuximab; continue this premedication at subsequent doses. Reconcile steroids with any antiemetic prescription to avoid duplication.
Ask specifically about earlier antibody reactions, red-meat allergy, tick bites and any cetuximab IgE result. Premedication does not eliminate severe or delayed reactions.
Use a local EGFR-inhibitor skin plan, moisturiser and sun protection; assess painful, infected or intolerable rash and nail changes promptly.

NCCP allows observation to cease after two reaction-free cetuximab doses, whereas current Erbitux SmPC section 4.2 requires monitoring during and for at least one hour after each infusion. Agree and document the governed observation plan; do not automatically remove observation.

Prescribe regimen-specific hydration and electrolyte replacement with fluid-balance review. The appropriate volume depends on kidney and cardiac status; a generic printed plan is not an intravenous-fluid prescription.
Review hearing, tinnitus and peripheral nerve symptoms before each cycle; damage can persist. Review nephrotoxic, ototoxic and other interacting medicines.

Record the dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (a medicine-processing enzyme) (DPD) result before the first fluorouracil exposure unless previously tested. Complete deficiency precludes fluorouracil; partial deficiency needs an individual starting dose and careful subsequent review.
Normal DPD testing cannot exclude all severe fluorouracil toxicity. Explain unexpectedly early or severe diarrhoea, mucositis, neurological symptoms and chest pain.
Write the actual infusion option, access arrangement, bag or pump changes and disconnect time. Do not equate four treatment days with a single universal pump duration.
Provide an individually prescribed diarrhoea plan and hand/foot care advice; severe or persistent symptoms require assessment rather than repeated self-treatment.
Arrange nutrition, weight and swallowing review early. Dietitian and speech and language therapy input should follow the person’s needs; swallowing safety cannot be inferred from a general leaflet.
Use the agreed mouth-care and dental plan. Report painful swallowing, mouth ulceration, weight loss or inability to drink before the next appointment.
Reconcile prescription, over-the-counter and complementary medicines. Discuss fertility, contraception and breastfeeding using the actual products and individual circumstances.
Confirm the hospital’s urgent contact and fever instructions. Infection, bleeding, severe diarrhoea, dehydration, chest pain or new breathlessness need prompt assessment, not the next routine review.
Use this high-risk plan for the platinum treatment day. Do not repeat its full antiemetic course automatically at weekly cetuximab-only visits.

Before signing: verify allergies, current medicines, interactions, renal / hepatic function, QT risk, sedation, prior response, total steroid exposure and the rescue-medicine duration. Do not duplicate medicines from another phase.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, persistent vomiting, diarrhoea, severe mouth pain or inability to drink. Chest pain during or after fluorouracil, or unusually early severe symptoms, needs urgent assessment even if dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (a medicine-processing enzyme) (DPD) testing was normal. Report breathing difficulty, swelling, faintness, spreading skin infection or painful eyes promptly. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.

Cetuximab with carboplatin and fluorouracil is used to treat squamous head and neck cancer when cisplatin is unsuitable. Your team explains the treatment aim, possible benefit and alternatives for your situation.

Cetuximab attaches to the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) on cells and blocks growth signals. It is combined with chemotherapy in this plan. Healthy skin and nails also depend on this pathway, explaining some of the characteristic rash, dryness and nail problems. This is a different treatment from checkpoint immunotherapy.
What to watch forTell staff immediately about itching, flushing, swelling, wheeze or faintness. Report skin infection, eye pain, new breathlessness or marked cramps.

Carboplatin interferes with DNA repair and cell division. Its dose is calculated from kidney function. Blood counts can fall, including platelets that help stop bleeding. It is a different prescription from cisplatin.
What to watch forReport fever, unusual bruising or bleeding, marked tiredness or an infusion reaction.

Fluorouracil, often shortened to 5-FU, interferes with the building blocks used to make DNA and RNA, which cells need to grow. It runs through a vein over the prescribed hours. Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) is an enzyme that breaks it down. Testing for DPD deficiency before treatment reduces risk but cannot rule out every severe reaction.
What to watch forReport severe diarrhoea, mouth sores, chest pain, sudden confusion, sore palms or soles, or unexpectedly early severe symptoms.

Your team confirms the active stage and dates. The full treatment guide explains each step.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.

Carboplatin is given on Day 1, fluorouracil on Days 1–4, and cetuximab on Days 1, 8 and 15, for up to 6 cycles every 21 days. Review determines what happens afterwards. Your team confirms any treatment after the combination phase; continuing cetuximab needs an agreed prescription and calendar.
These cetuximab-only visits remain part of the same combination cycle. Continue the skin, allergy and symptom checks; use the prescribed visit-specific support plan.
Visits within a cycle are not separate courses. The team records delays, omitted doses and any change of plan. A stamp records completed treatment; it does not authorise the next dose.
Required regimen tests, symptom-triggered investigations and cancer-response tests serve different purposes. Ask who books each test and who explains the result.
Checks infection-fighting cells, oxygen-carrying cells and platelets.
Guide safe treatment and identify organ problems.

Checks for reduced ability to break down fluorouracil; results affect treatment choice or dose. Testing cannot exclude every severe reaction. Kidney impairment can affect one blood-based test, so the team chooses the appropriate method.
Carboplatin dose is calculated from kidney filtration. A measured test is preferred where feasible; the team chooses a valid method and reassesses significant changes.
Investigates hearing loss or tinnitus and helps judge platinum-related risk.
Records the heart’s electrical activity. New chest symptoms require assessment even after a reassuring earlier test.
Detects mineral changes caused by cetuximab; low levels may cause cramps, weakness or heart-rhythm problems.
Assesses the cancer rather than whether a treatment-day blood count is safe.
Locally advanced or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma when cisplatin is contraindicated or not tolerated.
Blood and organ checksNCCP

Full blood count, kidney and liver tests and magnesium; kidney filtration assessment for carboplatin; DPD testing before fluorouracil unless already tested. Review previous antibody reactions, red-meat allergy, tick bites and any cetuximab allergy tests. Hearing tests and an ECG for compromised heart function are arranged when indicated.

Full blood count, kidney and liver tests and magnesium before each cycle, with a current kidney result for carboplatin calculation. Review hearing, nerves, skin, eyes, bowel symptoms and any reactions; report changes before every weekly cetuximab visit. The team may reassess kidney filtration if function changes.
Report new symptoms promptly; extra tests may be needed.
A held or changed dose needs a new clinical review and relevant repeat results.

Electrolytes including magnesium and calcium are checked monthly for 2 months after the final cetuximab. Continue review of unresolved skin, blood, hearing, nerve, mouth and nutritional problems. Examinations and scans follow the individually agreed cancer plan.
Treatment and appointmentsNCCP
Confirm the diagnosis, aim, prescription and actual calendar.

Cetuximab starts with a 400 mg/m² loading dose over 120 minutes, then 250 mg/m² over 60 minutes weekly. Chemotherapy starts at least 1 hour after cetuximab finishes. Carboplatin is infused over 30 minutes on Day 1 at a kidney-calculated target exposure of AUC 5. Fluorouracil 1,000 mg/m² is infused over 16–22 hours daily on Days 1–4, or 2,000 mg/m² over 48 hours twice. Plan for monitoring during and for at least 1 hour after each cetuximab infusion under the current medicine information; confirm the observation plan with your unit.
Follow the written home plan and keep pump or line appointments where applicable.
Record the last dose and follow-up appointments.
Mouth, weight and swallowingNCCP
Review oral health, weight, nutrition and safe swallowing.
Discuss mouth pain, intake, weight and hydration.
Report poor drinking, choking or weight loss promptly.
Dietitian and swallowing plans change with symptoms and recovery.
Continue dental, nutritional and swallowing support when needed.
Cancer assessmentNCCP
Agree staging, pathology and any relevant disease tests.
Discuss symptoms and the planned response review.
Scans or examinations may be added if symptoms require them.
The team sets imaging and cancer-assessment timing.
No universal imaging interval or routine tumour-marker panel is imposed by this regimen.
Ask / act: Confirm active medicines, written support plan and review criteria.

Who should I contact if an expected appointment has not arrived?

There are no guaranteed “safe days”. Your prescription and team’s instructions take priority. Contact the team about new symptoms rather than waiting for a scheduled visit.
Daily 16–22-hour fluorouracil on Days 1–4, or two 48-hour infusions; confirm the prescribed pump timetable. Check the pump appointments and contact the unit for problems.
Cetuximab is due on Days 8 and 15 after review. Other days are not automatically free of side effects. Report diarrhoea, mouth pain, rash, allergy symptoms or poor drinking before each visit.
Continue symptom monitoring and arrange the blood tests required for the next cycle. Ask for revised dates after any hold or delay.
From preparing the line to coming home after disconnection. Your team arranges the appointments and shows you what to do.
Your team selects the access device and teaches its care, including a port or peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) if used.
Daily 16–22-hour fluorouracil on Days 1–4, or two 48-hour infusions; confirm the prescribed pump timetable.
Only trained staff connect, program or change the infusion. Do not calculate or alter the rate yourself.
Call for leakage, pain, swelling, damage, disconnection, unexpected completion or a pump that appears not to run. Follow the unit’s device-specific emergency instructions.
Completion depends on the actual start time and chosen infusion duration. Do not disconnect or reconnect the line yourself.
A line may remain between treatments. Keep dressing, flushing and review appointments and report redness, pain, fever or swelling.

A port is a small chamber beneath the skin, usually on the chest, attached to a tube ending in a large vein. A special needle goes through the skin into the port when it is used. A PICC enters a vein in the upper arm; a short section remains outside under a dressing. Both can deliver a home infusion. Your team helps choose the device and teaches its care.

Tell the team about allergies, blood thinners, infections and any other cancer medicines. Follow the instructions about eating, drinking and transport; do not stop medicines yourself. Port placement uses local anaesthetic, sometimes with sedation or general anaesthetic. The team explains the procedure and risks, including infection, bleeding, clots and insertion complications. Ask how to manage discomfort, protect the wound and resume activity. Report increasing pain, redness, swelling, discharge or fever.

The nurse checks the line and treatment, secures the connection and dressing, and starts the pump. Before leaving, you should have the disconnection location and time, contact numbers including out of hours, and the written spill instructions. Ask to be shown what normal pump progress looks like. You do not need to calculate a rate.

Use the supplied carrier and the position recommended for your pump. Keep tubing free from pulling and kinks. Ask how to place the pump safely for sleep and how to protect the line and dressing when washing. Do not immerse it or swim. Avoid direct heat and cold. An elastomeric pump has a balloon that shrinks slowly and may have no alarm; an electronic pump has different instructions. Follow the instructions for the device you actually receive.

Keep the appointment even if the pump looks empty, unless the team changes the plan. Staff check the pump and line and arrange safe disposal. After flushing and other line care as required, the port needle may be removed and a small dressing applied. The implanted port stays in place until a separate removal procedure is arranged. A PICC remains in place and needs scheduled dressing and flushing care.

Call the team immediately if the pump leaks, is damaged, finishes unexpectedly early, appears not to run, or the line disconnects. Follow the emergency or spill steps you have been specifically taught, including use of a clamp if instructed. Do not reconnect, change settings or disconnect the pump yourself. Keep other people away from leaked medicine. If medicine touches skin, rinse it off and wash with soap and water, then seek advice.

Contact oncology immediately for pain or swelling around the line, a wet/loose dressing, redness, fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell. A painful swollen arm or neck needs urgent advice. Severe chest pain, major breathing difficulty or collapse: call 112 / 999. Do not wait for pump disconnection or the next clinic visit.
Agree the arrangements with your oncology team.
Bring your medicines and allergy list, test dates, treatment calendar and actual emergency contacts. Tell the unit about swallowing, hearing, mobility, transport or communication needs.
Check the next treatment and test dates, medicines, pump or line appointments, and who to contact if unwell. Have the team replace and verify every example phone number on the wallet card.
Ask about transport, work, costs, caring responsibilities, an interpreter or a support person. Keep changes to the plan in one record.

Ask for one list separating prevention medicines, rescue treatment and regular medicines. The schedule must match this treatment and visit. Record what you take and whether it helps; do not double a dose, restart an old prescription or add medicines without checking.

This platinum-containing combination needs an agreed anti-sickness plan. Take prevention medicines at the stated times and keep rescue instructions available. Contact the team for persistent vomiting or inability to drink.

An antihistamine and corticosteroid are given before cetuximab to reduce reaction risk. They do not prevent every reaction. Report itching, flushing, swelling, wheeze, dizziness or faintness immediately, including symptoms that start after leaving the unit.

Use the skin-care plan from the team, including moisturising and sun protection. Report painful cracks, inflamed nails, pus or spreading redness. Eye pain or visual change needs prompt review. Keep prescribed blood tests for magnesium and other minerals; supplements must follow clinical advice.
Tell the team early about reduced intake or weight loss. A dietitian can adapt food texture, supplements and intake goals. Follow an individual fluid plan, especially with kidney or heart problems.

Follow the mouth-care and pain-relief plan. Report ulcers, thrush or swallowing difficulty early. Ask for a swallowing assessment if food or drinks make you cough or choke; do not assume a general food texture is safe for you.

Before treatment, discuss fertility, contraception, pregnancy and breastfeeding, including medicine-specific precautions after treatment. Bring all prescription, over-the-counter and herbal medicines to review. The team must check interactions and allergies.
Keep the pathology, stage and agreed treatment aim with your records.

Ask which head or neck site the cancer started in, what the biopsy shows, how far it has spread and how previous treatment affects the options. HPV/p16 tests apply to some tumour sites; they are different from tests of chemotherapy safety.
Treatment of locally advanced or metastatic squamous cell cancer of the head and neck when cisplatin cannot be used or tolerated.

A scan or a tumour-specific test assesses the cancer. Blood counts and kidney or liver tests assess treatment safety. DPD testing concerns fluorouracil metabolism and is not a measure of cancer response.
The consent discussion sets out the personal aim and boundaries.

Cetuximab with carboplatin and fluorouracil is used to treat squamous head and neck cancer when cisplatin is unsuitable. Your team explains the treatment aim, possible benefit and alternatives for your situation. Ask about reasonable alternatives, including supportive care, and which outcomes matter most to you. A research result cannot predict an individual outcome.

The team may delay, reduce, omit or stop a medicine after symptoms or test results, a change in benefit or your preference. Record which medicine is affected and what is required before restarting. Do not use an old prescription to restart treatment.

Surgery or radiotherapy may have a separate role, but they are not automatically added to this infusion calendar. For a locally advanced plan, ask whether any part of treatment is outside its current licensed indication and why it is recommended.
Use the medicine schedule and logistics pages for the exact visit pattern.

Check that the treatment name, planned tests, support medicines, transport and urgent contacts are correct. Explain any previous infusion reaction or change in your health before the medicine is prepared.
A missed or held dose is not a completed dose. Ask for revised blood-test, treatment and pump dates where relevant. The team must clarify whether an omitted weekly dose changes later dates.
Record the actual date and medicines received, dose changes, test results and symptoms. The wallet is a brief portable record; the passport holds more detail and does not replace hospital records.
Symptoms do not follow a guaranteed calendar.

Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, persistent vomiting, diarrhoea, severe mouth pain or inability to drink. Chest pain during or after fluorouracil, or unusually early severe symptoms, needs urgent assessment even if DPD testing was normal. Report breathing difficulty, swelling, faintness, spreading skin infection or painful eyes promptly. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency.

Keep prevention, rescue and regular medicines separately labelled. Note doses actually taken and whether symptoms improve. Check new prescription, over-the-counter and herbal medicines with the team; do not add or repeat old courses without advice.

Report numbness, tingling, weakness, falls, difficulty doing buttons or changes in walking. Describe what you can no longer do, not just a symptom score. The team may need to change treatment before symptoms worsen.
This is the home for detailed mouth and dental advice.
Use the prescribed gentle oral-care and pain-relief plan. Report ulcers, infection, bleeding or pain that affects eating or drinking. Check with oncology before dental procedures.

If you have had head and neck radiation, tell your dentist before invasive treatment. Continue the advised preventive care because effects on saliva, teeth and healing can persist. If you have not had radiation, follow the plan for your current treatment.
Adapt the plan to what you can manage safely.

Record changes in weight and what limits eating: soreness, taste change, dry mouth, nausea or fatigue may need different help. A dietitian can adapt meals, supplements or feeding support. Do not wait for substantial weight loss to ask for review.

Contact the team for persistent vomiting, dizziness, much less urine, inability to drink or severe diarrhoea. Fluid goals depend on kidney and heart health. If a feeding tube is needed, ask for training, supplies and a clear problem-contact route.
Protect safe swallowing and make communication easier.

Report coughing or choking with food or drinks, a wet voice after swallowing, food sticking or repeated chest infections. Ask for speech and language assessment; use only the textures and exercises recommended for you.
Tell the team about hearing, speech or voice changes. Request written instructions, an interpreter, communication aids or help involving a support person when useful.
Use the support available around you.

Discuss the level of activity you can manage, work, travel and help at home. Ask for assessment if fatigue, pain, weakness or falls disrupt ordinary activities. Bring practical barriers to appointments into the discussion.

Ask about fertility preservation before treatment and specific pregnancy, contraception and breastfeeding precautions. Tell the team about anxiety, body-image, sexual or relationship concerns; support can be tailored to your priorities.
Ask for help with smoking cessation and discuss alcohol with the team. Mouth symptoms, medicines and recovery may affect what is appropriate for you.
Finishing scheduled doses and recovering are different milestones.
Record who arranges examinations, scans and any tumour-specific tests, and who explains the results. A general reference calendar does not set an appointment or mean a scan is overdue.

Keep the regimen name, last treatment date, current medicines and unresolved side effects available. Tell future clinicians about any earlier head and neck radiotherapy, platinum-related hearing or kidney problems, and significant infusion reactions.
Essential information should remain usable on paper.

Use the passport for the fuller record and the wallet card for the treatment name, contacts and actual completed cycles. Its QR opens this treatment’s information; it does not contain a personal medical record or update paper stamps.
Every example telephone number must be replaced and checked by the treating service before patient use. Add daytime, out-of-hours and backup contacts and keep them accessible to a support person.

Read the full handbook in its chapter sequence. The treatment, symptom, contact and practical information does not require scanning a QR or following a hyperlink. Add questions to the passport and bring it to review.
The EXTREME study tested adding cetuximab to platinum and fluorouracil for recurrent or metastatic squamous head and neck cancer.

The study supports this approach in an appropriate setting. The reported results pooled the platinum options; they are not a separate randomised survival estimate for this particular platinum or for a curative treatment plan. Population: Recurrent or metastatic disease; the study used either cisplatin or carboplatin. Comparison: Platinum and fluorouracil with or without cetuximab. Study populations and individual circumstances differ. The study does not establish that cisplatin and carboplatin give identical outcomes. The current regimen and an individually agreed plan govern treatment duration.

Cetuximab with carboplatin and fluorouracil is used to treat squamous head and neck cancer when cisplatin is unsuitable. Your team explains the treatment aim, possible benefit and alternatives for your situation. Ask your team to write down the individual aim and explain reasonable alternatives, their burdens and the uncertainties before you decide.

Carboplatin is given on Day 1, fluorouracil on Days 1–4, and cetuximab on Days 1, 8 and 15, for up to 6 cycles every 21 days. Review determines what happens afterwards. Your team confirms any treatment after the combination phase; continuing cetuximab needs an agreed prescription and calendar. Full blood count, kidney and liver tests and magnesium before each cycle, with a current kidney result for carboplatin calculation. Review hearing, nerves, skin, eyes, bowel symptoms and any reactions; report changes before every weekly cetuximab visit. The team may reassess kidney filtration if function changes. Confirm the actual dates with your unit.

Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, persistent vomiting, diarrhoea, severe mouth pain or inability to drink. Chest pain during or after fluorouracil, or unusually early severe symptoms, needs urgent assessment even if DPD testing was normal. Report breathing difficulty, swelling, faintness, spreading skin infection or painful eyes promptly. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency. Have the team replace the example numbers with verified daytime, out-of-hours and backup contacts before using the card.

Your team reviews symptoms, test results, treatment benefit and your priorities. Ask when cancer-response assessment is planned and what would lead to a change. A delay or omitted dose must be recorded and does not count as treatment received.

Ask for a written support-medicine plan and early help with mouth pain, eating, drinking, swallowing, skin or nerve symptoms. Tell the team about travel, work, caring and communication needs. Dietitian, speech and language, nursing and other support can be arranged according to your needs.

Give an antihistamine and a corticosteroid at least one hour before cetuximab; continue this premedication at subsequent doses. Reconcile steroids with any antiemetic prescription to avoid duplication.
Ask specifically about earlier antibody reactions, red-meat allergy, tick bites and any cetuximab IgE result. Premedication does not eliminate severe or delayed reactions.
Use a local EGFR-inhibitor skin plan, moisturiser and sun protection; assess painful, infected or intolerable rash and nail changes promptly.

NCCP allows observation to cease after two reaction-free cetuximab doses, whereas current Erbitux SmPC section 4.2 requires monitoring during and for at least one hour after each infusion. Agree and document the governed observation plan; do not automatically remove observation.

Carboplatin dosing uses the selected AUC and a verified absolute kidney-function estimate in mL/min. Indexed laboratory estimated glomerular filtration rate (kidney filtration) (eGFR) must not be substituted directly into Calvert dosing.
Check the kidney-function method, creatinine timing, prior platinum exposure and any previous hypersensitivity. Severe low counts and renal impairment may change the next treatment plan.

Record the dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (a medicine-processing enzyme) (DPD) result before the first fluorouracil exposure unless previously tested. Complete deficiency precludes fluorouracil; partial deficiency needs an individual starting dose and careful subsequent review.
Normal DPD testing cannot exclude all severe fluorouracil toxicity. Explain unexpectedly early or severe diarrhoea, mucositis, neurological symptoms and chest pain.
Write the actual infusion option, access arrangement, bag or pump changes and disconnect time. Do not equate four treatment days with a single universal pump duration.
Provide an individually prescribed diarrhoea plan and hand/foot care advice; severe or persistent symptoms require assessment rather than repeated self-treatment.
Arrange nutrition, weight and swallowing review early. Dietitian and speech and language therapy input should follow the person’s needs; swallowing safety cannot be inferred from a general leaflet.
Use the agreed mouth-care and dental plan. Report painful swallowing, mouth ulceration, weight loss or inability to drink before the next appointment.
Reconcile prescription, over-the-counter and complementary medicines. Discuss fertility, contraception and breastfeeding using the actual products and individual circumstances.
Confirm the hospital’s urgent contact and fever instructions. Infection, bleeding, severe diarrhoea, dehydration, chest pain or new breathlessness need prompt assessment, not the next routine review.
Use this high-risk plan for the platinum treatment day. Do not repeat its full antiemetic course automatically at weekly cetuximab-only visits.

Record each cycle separately. Each medicine has its own symptom table. Mark the worst symptoms since your last review, when they occurred and what they stopped you doing. Overlapping symptoms can be recorded under more than one medicine; you do not have to identify the cause.

These are patient-language severity prompts, not a validated questionnaire or a formal Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grading tool. Your team assigns the clinical grade. Serious symptoms override the columns: call without waiting to decide a severity level.
Use a new record sheet for each cycle or review. Copy or print another sheet when needed; the number of sheets does not prescribe the length of treatment.
Record the date, medicines actually received, delays or omissions, test results and concerns with your team. Use a separate record for any changed treatment phase.

required_units.text: Space for your own cycle or review record, questions and notes, followed by your treatment card.
Carboplatin + fluorouracil after nasopharyngeal chemoradiotherapyNational Cancer Control Programme (NCCP) 00552

Record each cycle separately. Each medicine has its own symptom table. Mark the worst symptoms since your last review, when they occurred and what they stopped you doing. Overlapping symptoms can be recorded under more than one medicine; you do not have to identify the cause.

These are patient-language severity prompts, not a validated questionnaire or a formal Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grading tool. Your team assigns the clinical grade. Serious symptoms override the columns: call without waiting to decide a severity level.
Use a new record sheet for each cycle or review. Copy or print another sheet when needed; the number of sheets does not prescribe the length of treatment.
Record the date, medicines actually received, delays or omissions, test results and concerns with your team. Use a separate record for any changed treatment phase.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, persistent vomiting, diarrhoea, severe mouth pain or inability to drink. Chest pain during or after fluorouracil, or unusually early severe symptoms, needs urgent assessment even if dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (a medicine-processing enzyme) (DPD) testing was normal. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.

This chemotherapy is an additional treatment after chemoradiotherapy for nasopharyngeal cancer. It aims to treat cancer cells that may remain. The team explains the expected benefit and burden for you, including recovery from the earlier treatment.

Carboplatin interferes with DNA repair and cell division. Its dose is calculated from kidney function. Blood counts can fall, including platelets that help stop bleeding. It is a different prescription from cisplatin.
What to watch forReport fever, unusual bruising or bleeding, marked tiredness or an infusion reaction.

Fluorouracil, often shortened to 5-FU, interferes with the building blocks used to make DNA and RNA, which cells need to grow. It runs through a vein over the prescribed hours. Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) is an enzyme that breaks it down. Testing for DPD deficiency before treatment reduces risk but cannot rule out every severe reaction.
What to watch forReport severe diarrhoea, mouth sores, chest pain, sudden confusion, sore palms or soles, or unexpectedly early severe symptoms.
The drawings are simplified explanations of drug action, not anatomical pictures or a prediction of response.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.

After recovery, adjuvant chemotherapy is planned to begin 4 weeks after completion of weekly carboplatin with radiotherapy (NCCP 00419). Carboplatin is given on Day 1 and fluorouracil over Days 1–4, every 28 days for up to 3 cycles. The treating team confirms readiness and dates.
Visits within a cycle are not separate courses. The team records delays, omitted doses and any change of plan. A stamp records completed treatment; it does not authorise the next dose.
Required regimen tests, symptom-triggered investigations and cancer-response tests serve different purposes. Ask who books each test and who explains the result.
Checks infection-fighting cells, oxygen-carrying cells and platelets.
Guide safe treatment and identify organ problems.

Checks for reduced ability to break down fluorouracil; results affect treatment choice or dose. Testing cannot exclude every severe reaction. Kidney impairment can affect one blood-based test, so the team chooses the appropriate method.
Carboplatin dose is calculated from kidney filtration. A measured test is preferred where feasible; the team chooses a valid method and reassesses significant changes.
Investigates hearing loss or tinnitus and helps judge platinum-related risk.
Assesses the cancer rather than whether a treatment-day blood count is safe.
Adjuvant chemotherapy after chemoradiotherapy for locally advanced stage III or IV nasopharyngeal carcinoma when cisplatin is contraindicated or not tolerated.
Blood and organ checksNCCP

Full blood count, kidney and liver tests, a kidney filtration assessment to calculate carboplatin, and DPD testing before the first fluorouracil unless already tested. Measured kidney filtration is preferred where feasible. Hearing assessment is arranged when indicated. Confirm recovery from chemoradiotherapy, swallowing, weight and intake.

Full blood count, kidney and liver tests before each cycle. Review mouth soreness, swallowing, weight, intake and painful palms or soles; hearing and nerve symptoms also need review. If kidney function changes, the carboplatin calculation may need reassessment.
Report new symptoms promptly; extra tests may be needed.
A held or changed dose needs a new clinical review and relevant repeat results.

Continue recovery and follow-up after chemoradiotherapy and chemotherapy, including mouth, dental, swallowing, nutritional, hearing or nerve problems. Examinations, scans and any tumour-specific tests follow the agreed nasopharyngeal cancer plan; this regimen does not prescribe a universal interval.
Treatment and appointmentsNCCP
Confirm the diagnosis, aim, prescription and actual calendar.

Carboplatin is infused over 30 minutes on Day 1. Its dose is calculated from kidney function using a target exposure called AUC 5. Fluorouracil 1,000 mg/m² per day is given as a continuous 96-hour infusion, or as the source-listed daily 22-hour option on Days 1–4. Your unit confirms the actual prescription, pump changes and disconnection time.
Follow the written home plan and keep pump or line appointments where applicable.
Record the last dose and follow-up appointments.
Mouth, weight and swallowingNCCP
Review oral health, weight, nutrition and safe swallowing.
Discuss mouth pain, intake, weight and hydration.
Report poor drinking, choking or weight loss promptly.
Dietitian and swallowing plans change with symptoms and recovery.
Continue dental, nutritional and swallowing support when needed.
Cancer assessmentNCCP
Agree staging, pathology and any relevant disease tests.
Discuss symptoms and the planned response review.
Scans or examinations may be added if symptoms require them.
The team sets imaging and cancer-assessment timing.
No universal imaging interval or routine tumour-marker panel is imposed by this regimen.
Ask / act: Confirm active medicines, written support plan and review criteria.
